name: Elijah
bio:
Elijah the Tishbite, from Gilead, bursts into the narrative without introduction or genealogy, announcing to King Ahab, "As the LORD, the God of Israel, lives, whom I serve, there will be neither dew nor rain in the next few years except at my word" — a direct challenge to Baal, the storm-and-fertility god Ahab and Jezebel had enthroned in Israel (1 Kings 17:1).

## 📖 Core Story: Sustained by Ravens and a Widow's Faith

At the LORD's command, Elijah hid by the Kerith Ravine east of the Jordan, where ravens brought him bread and meat morning and evening and he drank from the brook — until the drought he had announced dried the brook itself up (1 Kings 17:2-7). The LORD then sent him to Zarephath, in Sidon, to a widow He had already commanded to supply him food. When Elijah found her gathering sticks at the town gate and asked for water and bread, she told him she had only a handful of flour and a little oil left — enough for one last meal before she and her son would starve to death. Elijah told her not to be afraid, but to make him a small loaf first, promising that "the jar of flour will not be used up and the jug of oil will not run dry until the day the LORD sends rain on the land." She did as he said, and the flour and oil miraculously did not run out, sustaining her household for many days (1 Kings 17:8-16).

Later, the widow's son fell ill and stopped breathing. In anguish, she confronted Elijah, asking if he had come to bring her sin to remembrance by killing her son. Elijah carried the boy to his own room, laid him on the bed, and cried out to the LORD three times, stretching himself out over the child and pleading for his life to return. The LORD heard Elijah's cry, and the boy's life returned to him; Elijah carried him back down and presented him alive to his mother, who declared, "Now I know that you are a man of God and that the word of the LORD from your mouth is the truth" (1 Kings 17:17-24). ## 📖 Core Story: The Showdown on Mount Carmel

In the third year of the drought, the LORD sent Elijah to present himself to Ahab, promising rain. On the way, Elijah met Obadiah, Ahab's palace administrator, who had secretly hidden a hundred of the LORD's prophets from Jezebel's purge; after Obadiah nervously agreed to tell Ahab, Elijah finally stood face to face with the king. Ahab called him "you troubler of Israel," and Elijah shot back that it was Ahab's own family, by abandoning the LORD's commands and following Baal, who had brought the trouble (1 Kings 18:1-18).

Elijah summoned all Israel, along with the 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of Asherah who ate at Jezebel's table, to Mount Carmel. There he challenged the wavering people directly: "How long will you waver between two opinions? If the LORD is God, follow him; but if Baal is God, follow him." He proposed a contest: two bulls would be prepared as sacrifices, one for Baal's prophets and one for his own, each laid on wood with no fire lit beneath it — and whichever god answered by fire would be recognized as the true God. All the people agreed (1 Kings 18:19-24).

The prophets of Baal went first, calling on Baal from morning until noon, dancing around their altar, with no answer at all. Elijah taunted them mercilessly — maybe Baal was deep in thought, or busy, or traveling, or asleep and needed waking — and they shouted louder and slashed themselves with swords and spears until they bled, but still there was no response of any kind (1 Kings 18:25-29). Elijah then repaired the LORD's broken-down altar using twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel, dug a trench around it, arranged the wood and the bull, and — in a dramatic flourish that made any mundane explanation for what followed impossible — had the people drench the offering and the wood with twelve barrels of water, not once but three times, until the water filled the trench itself. Elijah then prayed a brief, simple prayer: "LORD, the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, let it be known today that you are God in Israel and that I am your servant... Answer me, LORD, answer me, so these people will know that you, LORD, are God, and that you are turning their hearts back again." Fire fell from the LORD and consumed the sacrifice, the wood, the stones, the soil, and even licked up the water in the trench. The people fell face down and cried, "The LORD — he is God! The LORD — he is God!" Elijah then had the prophets of Baal seized and put to death at the Kishon Valley (1 Kings 18:30-40).

Elijah told Ahab to eat and drink, for he could hear the sound of coming rain; he himself went to the top of Carmel, bent down with his face between his knees, and sent his servant to look toward the sea seven times before a cloud no bigger than a man's hand finally appeared. Elijah warned Ahab to hurry down before the rain stopped him, and moments later the sky grew black with clouds and a heavy rain began. With the power of the LORD upon him, Elijah tucked his cloak into his belt and ran ahead of Ahab's chariot all the way to Jezreel (1 Kings 18:41-46).

## 📖 Core Story: The Still Small Voice at Horeb

When Jezebel sent word threatening to kill him within a day, Elijah — who had just called down fire from heaven — fled for his life to Beersheba, then a day's journey into the wilderness, where he sat under a tree and asked to die: "It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers." An angel woke him twice with bread and water, and on that strength he walked forty days and nights to Horeb, the mountain of God (1 Kings 19:1-8).

There, in a cave, the LORD asked him, "What doest thou here, Elijah?" He answered that he had been very jealous for the LORD, that Israel had forsaken the covenant, torn down the altars, and killed the prophets, and that he alone was left and his own life was being hunted. The LORD told him to stand on the mountain, and a great wind tore the mountains apart, then an earthquake, then a fire passed — but the LORD was not in the wind, the earthquake, or the fire. After the fire came a still small voice, and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak and went to the entrance of the cave, where the voice asked him the same question again and received the same answer (1 Kings 19:9-14).

The LORD then sent him back by way of the wilderness of Damascus with a threefold commission: anoint Hazael king over Syria, anoint Jehu son of Nimshi king over Israel, and anoint Elisha son of Shaphat as prophet in his own place — assuring him he was not alone, for seven thousand in Israel had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19:15-18). Elijah found Elisha plowing with twelve yoke of oxen and threw his cloak over him; Elisha asked only to say goodbye to his parents first, then slaughtered his own oxen, burned his plowing equipment to cook the meat for the people, and left to become Elijah's attendant (1 Kings 19:19-21).
